episodes.title: Green Wood and Dry: Proverbs 26, Luke 23, Hebrews 9
episodes.summary: Episode one of Morning Mercies, joining the Navigators plan at month nine, day sixteen with the Old Testament track set aside. Proverbs 26:1-16 was taught as two clusters from Hezekiah's collection, the fool (Hebrew kesil, in every verse of 1-12 but verse 2) and the sluggard (13-16); the apparent contradiction of verses 4-5 was resolved with Matthew Poole (persons, times and circumstances) and R.C. Sproul (the answer depends on the situation, verse 5 as argument by absurdity), verse 11 with Gregory the Great's Pastoral Rule on lamenting sins without forsaking them (Peter quotes the proverb in 2 Peter 2:22), verse 12 as the chapter's turn, and the sluggard's lion with John Gill; application: name your lion. Luke 23:26-31 was the heart: Simon of Cyrene seized and carrying the cross 'behind Jesus' (Piper's observation, echoing Luke 9:23 and 14:27), Augustine's harmonization with John 19:17, Henry on the soldiers' self-serving relief, Mark 15:21 and Romans 16:13 on Rufus (Ferguson), the Jerusalem women's real grief and Jesus' redirection of it (Calvin: his death is the beginning of Jerusalem's evils, not the end; Spurgeon's 1876 sermon: weeping over the dying Saviour laments the remedy, not the disease), Hosea 10:8 in verse 30, the A.D. 70 siege, and the green and dry wood (Greek hugros and xeros, Ezekiel 20:47) read with Sproul and Matthew Henry as God's wrath falling on the innocent Son; application: be changed, not merely moved, by the cross. Hebrews 9:11-28 was placed in the letter's central argument (8:1-10:18) against the Day of Atonement: the better tent, his own blood, once for all, the red heifer of Numbers 19 and dead works (Chrysostom), the cleansed conscience set free to serve (Piper), diatheke as covenant and will (Calvin's point that the letter was written in Greek), Exodus 24:8, Christ appearing in God's presence as advocate (Calvin), the repeated hapax 'once', Isaiah 53:12 behind 'bear the sins of many', and the high priest coming out to an eagerly waiting people. The close linked tears and washing that do not change the life (Proverbs 26:11, the women, Hebrews 9:14) and judgment borne once by the green wood.
threads: Luke 23: tomorrow (23:32-37) reaches the crucifixion itself; the green and dry wood saying and Jesus' concern for Jerusalem's women and children can be recalled when he prays 'Father, forgive them'.
Simon of Cyrene's sons Alexander and Rufus, possibly the Rufus of Romans 16:13; worth a callback if Luke or Romans returns to them.

Hebrews: 9:11-28 ended on the once-for-all offering and the second appearing; 10:1-18 tomorrow completes the central argument that the one sacrifice needs no repeating. Calvin and Chrysostom both read 'many' in 9:28 broadly; Calvin's point that 'many' is opposed to 'one' was used, the wider debate was not opened.
Proverbs 26: verses 17-28 tomorrow turn to meddlers, quarrels, whisperers and lying lips; the fool and sluggard clusters and the 'wise in his own eyes' turn of verse 12 can frame them.

Running theme introduced: sorrow and cleansing that do not change the life (Gregory on the dog returning, the weeping women, a conscience purified to serve). Avoid repeating Gregory's dog image, Spurgeon's 'lament the remedy' line, and the 'name your lion' application.

episodes.title: Forgive Them: Proverbs 26, Luke 23, Hebrews 10
episodes.summary: Plan day 9-17. Proverbs 26:17-28 was taught as three movements: meddling and the joker who says 'I am only joking' (verses 17-19, with Matthew Poole and Matthew Henry on the needless danger of the meddler), fire and the whisperer or nirgan (verses 20-22, with Gill and Henry; application: do not add wood), and the glazed pot of smooth speech over a hateful heart (verses 23-26, Poole) closing with the pit and the rolling stone (verses 27-28, Henry). Luke 23:32-37 was the heart: the two criminals and Isaiah 53:12, Golgotha as the Skull, the prayer 'Father, forgive them' with its textual note, the hard question whether ignorance excuses (Gill: it did not; Spurgeon's 1890 sermon: 'we might have known'; Acts 3:17 and Pentecost as the prayer's answer), the lots of Psalm 22:18 and the sour wine of Psalm 69:21, and the three-fold taunt 'save yourself' with Matthew Henry; application: pray the first half of the prayer for one person who has wronged you. Hebrews 10:1-18 completed the central argument: shadow versus true form, repetition as a reminder of sins (Chrysostom, Piper), Psalm 40 and 'a body you have prepared', once for all sanctification, priests standing versus Christ seated (Poole), 'perfected for all time' as settled standing (Piper, Gill), and the Jeremiah 31 promise of sins remembered no more. The close tied 'save yourself' to the single sacrifice, and the pit and rolling stone of Proverbs 26:27 to the cross.
threads: Luke 23:38-43 tomorrow: the inscription over the cross and the penitent criminal; pick up that the taunt 'save yourself' came from rulers, soldiers and, in Luke, one criminal.
Hebrews 10:19-39 tomorrow turns from what Christ has done to how to draw near; the finished sacrifice and sitting priest set up 'let us draw near'.
Proverbs 27:1-14 tomorrow: boasting about tomorrow, flattery and friendship; the glaze over a hateful heart in 26:23-26 contrasts with the faithful wounds of a friend.

Running theme: forgiveness asked for, forgiveness secured, and the question whether we still remind others of their sins. Church father on Luke 23:34 was not verified today; try Augustine or Ambrose if sources load.
Avoid repeating today's illustrations: the meddler and the dog by the ears, wood for the fire, the glazed pot, the gambling soldiers, the medicine taken once.

episodes.title: Remember Me: Proverbs 27, Luke 23, Hebrews 10
episodes.summary: Plan day 9-18. Proverbs 27:1-14 was taught as loose pairs from Hezekiah's collection on tomorrow, praise, provocation, friendship and prudence: Matthew Henry (preparing for tomorrow versus presuming upon it, faithful rebukes over flattery that compliments in sin), John Gill (no man can assure himself of more than the present time) and Matthew Poole (the near neighbor near in affection); application: who may wound you faithfully. Luke 23:38-43 was the heart: the inscription, the second criminal's rebuke, confession and prayer, with Calvin (the most striking example of faith, life in death, the promise does not remove present pain), Gill on great faith, Augustine via the Cambridge Bible (mercy prayed so that misery might pray), the words amen, semeron and paradeisos (a Persian royal garden), Spurgeon's 1889 sermon The Believing Thief (trust is the saving act, the speediness of it), a Ligonier article on 'today', and Henry on why late repentance is seldom true; application: pray the thief's prayer today. Hebrews 10:19-39 was taught as the turn from doctrine to exhortation with three 'let us' verbs (draw near, hold fast, consider one another), Chrysostom on the curtain and on assembling together, Calvin on the willful sin of verse 26 as apostasy rather than ordinary falling (against Novatus), the former days, Habakkuk 2:3-4, and Calvin on patience. The close tied the thief's 'remember me' to 'I will remember their sins no more', Proverbs' 'do not boast about tomorrow' to Jesus' 'today', and the thief's faithful wound to Hebrews 10:24.
threads: Luke 23:44-49 tomorrow: darkness, the torn temple curtain (already linked to Hebrews 10:20), 'Father, into your hands', the centurion. The curtain image was introduced today.
Hebrews 11:1-16 tomorrow begins the faith chapter; today's 'the righteous shall live by faith' (Habakkuk 2:4) and the call to endurance set it up.
Proverbs 27:15-27 tomorrow: the quarrelsome wife, iron sharpening iron (pick up the faithful friend and stirring one another up), the care of flocks.

Running theme: remembered and forgotten sins (the thief's prayer, Jeremiah 31 in Hebrews 10:17), today versus tomorrow. Do not repeat Spurgeon's 'speediness' line, Calvin's 'life in death' list, or the 'friend who wounds' application.

Church father on the thief was only paraphrased (Augustine via the Cambridge Bible); try to verify Chrysostom's homily on the cross and the thief or Ambrose on Luke in a public-domain text. Piper pages returned 403 this run.

Hard question handled: deathbed repentance is a rescue, not a loophole (Henry); the Hebrews 10:26 warning was read as apostasy per Calvin, with the Baptist and Presbyterian note on baptism kept to a sentence.

episodes.title: Into Your Hands: Proverbs 27, Luke 23, Hebrews 11
episodes.summary: Plan day 9-19. Proverbs 27:15-27 was taught as the dripping roof of a quarrelsome home (Gill), iron sharpening iron as friction that makes sparks (Poole, Gill, tied to Hebrews 10:24), the mirror of the heart, death never satisfied, praise as a crucible, and the closing farming poem on knowing the face of your flocks (Henry, Poole); application: look closely at what is truly yours to tend. Luke 23:44-49 was the heart: the noon darkness that was no natural eclipse at a Passover full moon (Gill, Cambridge Bible), the torn curtain as the Shechinah leaving the temple and as the way opened (Cambridge Bible, Hebrews 10), Luke's last prayer from Psalm 31:5 with the added word Father and the verb paratithemai as a deposit (Gill on his human soul, Pulpit Commentary on the centurion hearing the prayer), Spurgeon's 1889 sermon (dying is going home to our Father), the centurion's glorifying God and the crowds beating their breasts as the answer to Luke 23:28, and the watching women; application: pray the commitment prayer at night. Hebrews 11:1-16 was placed as the answer to Habakkuk 2:4 in 10:38, with hupostasis and elegchos (Henry, Sproul via Ligonier: faith's object has a track record), Abel (Chrysostom), Enoch, Noah, Abraham's tents and the city with foundations, Sarah, the hard verse 13 on dying without receiving, and God not ashamed to be called their God (Gill, Poole, Chrysostom). The close linked the Father who receives with the God who owns, and tending with trusting.
threads: Luke 23:50-56 tomorrow: Joseph of Arimathea and the burial; the women who watched from a distance in 23:49 are the ones who prepare spices.
Hebrews 11:17-31 tomorrow: Abraham and Isaac, Moses; the strangers and exiles theme and the city with foundations can be recalled.
Proverbs 28:1-14 tomorrow: the wicked who flee when no one pursues; contrast with the shepherd who knows his flock.

Running theme: handing over versus holding (Father, receive my spirit; strangers who hold the world loosely). Avoid repeating the bedtime prayer application, Spurgeon's 'going home' line, the iron-sparks image, and the 'know the face of your flock' application.
Calvin and Piper pages could not be fetched today; try again for the Gospel segments. Chrysostom on Hebrews 11 verses 14 to 16 was verified only from Homily 24.

episodes.title: The Borrowed Tomb: Proverbs 28, Luke 23, Hebrews 11
episodes.summary: Plan day 9-20. Proverbs 28:1-14 was taught through the theme of what a person is like when no one is watching: the wicked who flee when no one pursues and the bold righteous (Gill, Matthew Henry, Pulpit Commentary), the prayer of the one who refuses God's law in verse 9 (Henry, Poole), and verse 13 with confession joined to forsaking (Henry, Poole, Pulpit); application: bring into the light what you are covering. Luke 23:50-56 was the heart: Joseph of Arimathea as a council member who had not consented and was waiting for the kingdom, Chrysostom on his sudden boldness after the death of Christ, Spurgeon's 1888 sermon A Royal Funeral (God can make a coward bold), the sindon linen (Cambridge Bible), the new tomb (Gill, Spurgeon, Pulpit), the hurried burial on the day of Preparation (Henry), Calvin that the burial was the work of God and the new tomb points to newness of life, and the women keeping the Sabbath; application: do the next thing in front of you without waiting to feel brave. Hebrews 11:17-31 followed Abraham's reasoning that God could raise Isaac (Henry, Chrysostom Homily 25, Poole, a Ligonier devotional), the three deathbed blessings, Moses and the reproach of Christ (Poole, Gill, Cambridge, Henry), Passover, the Red Sea, Jericho and Rahab. The close tied the two Josephs and their burial hopes and Proverbs' conscience at rest to the courage in Luke and Hebrews.
threads: Luke 24:1-12 tomorrow: the women return with spices; the new tomb and the sindon linen from today can be recalled at the empty grave.
Hebrews 11:32-40 tomorrow: the list runs on to those mistreated who did not receive what was promised; pick up Hebrews 11:13 and today's Moses and Rahab.
Proverbs 28:15-28 tomorrow: rulers, the wicked in power, and more on concealing and confessing.

Running theme: boldness from a conscience at rest, and acting before feeling brave. Avoid repeating Spurgeon's coward-bold-as-a-lion line, Chrysostom on Joseph's love and courage, the confess-and-forsake application, and the 'next thing in front of you' application.
Piper and Sproul on these passages could not be verified; Calvin on Hebrews 11 was not reached. Try again.

episodes.title: Why Seek the Living: Proverbs 28, Luke 24, Hebrews 11
episodes.summary: Proverbs 28:15-28 was taught in clusters: the wicked ruler as lion and bear (a shepherd turned predator), integrity versus sudden fall, work versus hurrying to be rich, then the heart of the section in verses 23 to 27 on rebuke over flattery (Matthew Henry, John Gill), trusting your own mind (Matthew Poole) and the open hand (Gill); application: an open ear and an open hand. Luke 24:1-12 was the heart: the women who kept the Sabbath and came at deep dawn with spices, the angels' call to remember Jesus' words in Galilee, Joanna and the named witnesses, Chrysostom on the women seeing him first, the apostles' persistent disbelief (leros, idle tale, per the Cambridge Bible and Ellicott), and Peter who arose and ran (Henry), with Spurgeon's 1873 sermon on the fragrant grave; application: go and look when faith will not come. Hebrews 11:32-40 covered the closing roll call, the two halves of rescue and suffering, the better resurrection (Gill, Cambridge Bible), the world not worthy and the saints waiting for us (Chrysostom Homily 28, Gill, Barnes).
threads: Luke 24:13-27 tomorrow: the Emmaus road; the theme of remembering and Jesus' own words from today's angels can be picked up when he opens the Scriptures himself.
Hebrews 12:1-13 tomorrow: the 'therefore' after the roll call and the saints who wait for us; the race and discipline.
Proverbs 29:1-14 tomorrow: stiff necks, rulers and justice; pick up the closed ear and rebuke themes from 28:23.

Running theme: faithfulness without sight, and women and the dead (Hebrews 11:35 and Luke 24). Avoid repeating Spurgeon's fragrant grave line, Henry's Peter 'ran from his Master' line, Chrysostom's 'wait for the brethren', and the open hand and ear application.
No Calvin, Sproul, Piper or other modern conservative could be verified this run (pages unreachable); try again for Emmaus.

episodes.title: We Had Hoped: Proverbs 29, Luke 24, Hebrews 12
episodes.summary: Proverbs 29:1-14 was taught as part of Hezekiah's collection: the stiff neck as a resisting ox (Gill) broken suddenly beyond healing, rulers and justice for the poor (verses 2, 4, 7, 13-14, with the oppressor and poor man sharing God's light), flattery as a net, the fool's unrestrained anger (Henry's dunghill, the Pulpit Commentary's 'command your temper'); application: who may correct you, yoke or gift. Luke 24:13-27 was the heart: the Emmaus road, Cleopas, eyes held (Henry), 'we had hoped' (elpizomen, imperfect), anoetoi and slow of heart (Henry, Bengel), 'was it not necessary' (edei), Moses and all the Prophets (Henry, Sproul), grace under ignorance (Ryle); application: tell him 'we had hoped'. Hebrews 12:1-13: the therefore after the roll call, martys, weight and clinging sin, archegos Jesus (Henry), paideia as fatherly training (Chrysostom on sonship and the athlete, Spurgeon 1855, Henry on peaceable fruit), straight paths for the lame. Closing tied Emmaus and Hebrews: God close in hard stretches, and bending the neck.
threads: Luke 24:28-35 tomorrow: the breaking of bread, eyes opened, and 'did not our hearts burn' (previewed today; do not repeat the order 'hearts first, then eyes').
Hebrews 12:14-29 tomorrow: pursue peace and holiness, Esau, Sinai and Zion, the shaking of heaven and earth.
Proverbs 29:15-27 tomorrow: the rod and reproof, vision, fear of man; connect to today's discipline and stiff neck.

Running theme: God close and unrecognized in hard stretches; receiving correction versus stiffening the neck. Avoid repeating Gill's ox, Henry's dunghill, Chrysostom's athlete, the 'we had hoped' application.
Not verified this run: Calvin (CCEL pages empty), a church father on Luke 24, Piper (403); try again tomorrow.

episodes.title: No Wine: Ecclesiastes 4, John 2:1-11, James 3:1-12
episodes.summary: Plan day 10-6. Ecclesiastes 4 was taught as the Preacher standing among the oppressed with no one to comfort them (Pulpit Commentary), envy as the engine of skill (Cambridge Bible), the handful of quietness against idleness (Henry), the lonely worker with no second, two better than one with the threefold cord (Cambridge Bible, Henry), and the fickle crowds around the youth-king. John 2:1-11 was the heart: Cana as the end of John's opening week, the shame of a wedding running out of wine (Spurgeon), Jesus as guest (Augustine), the hard saying about his hour (Gill, Poole, Barnes, Cambridge Bible, Chrysostom and Calvin paraphrased), Mary's word to the servants, the six purification jars, the master's joke made true (Cambridge Bible), the best wine last (Spurgeon), and the sign revealing glory (Gill); application: tell Christ what has run out and do what he says. James 3:1-12 covered teachers and stumbling (Calvin, Ellicott, Barnes), bit, rudder and fire, the untameable tongue (Calvin, Henry, Sproul via Ligonier), and blessing and cursing from one mouth (Calvin).

James 3:13-18 tomorrow: wisdom from above as the cure for the untamed tongue.
Ecclesiastes 5 tomorrow: guard your steps and your words in the house of God; recall the tongue.

Running theme: someone notices and comforts versus the tongue that wounds. Avoid repeating Mary's 'they have no wine' application, Spurgeon's best last, Augustine's water and wine, Calvin's hypocrisy line, and the threefold cord.

episodes.title: Zeal for the House: John 2:12-25, James 3:13-18, Ecclesiastes 5
episodes.summary: Plan day 10-7. Ecclesiastes 5 was taught in four movements: guarding your steps and words in the house of God (Matthew Henry, Pulpit Commentary, Gill), vows, the higher official watching over injustice, the insatiable love of money (Poole, Cambridge Bible), and wealth received as a gift of God. John 2:12-25 was the heart: the first Passover, the court of the Gentiles, the whip as symbol (Barnes, Pulpit, Chrysostom, Augustine), zeal from Psalm 69 and Spurgeon's Zeal of Christ, hieron versus naos, destroy this temple (Gill, Augustine, Sproul), and Jesus not entrusting himself to a sign-based faith (Pulpit, Gill, Henry). James 3:13-18 covered the two wisdoms, meekness in conduct (Gill, Barnes), bitter zeal as envy (Poole, Cambridge Bible), purity before peace (Poole, Cambridge Bible, Barnes), and the harvest of righteousness sown in peace. Ecclesiastes 6 tomorrow: the man who has everything and cannot enjoy it; recall wealth as gift.
Running theme: what is under the display. Avoid repeating the zeal-versus-bitter-zeal contrast, Henry's hasty prayer, and Poole's purity before peace.

episodes.title: The Wind and the Window: Ecclesiastes 6, John 3:1-15, James 4:1-10
episodes.summary: Plan day 10-8. Ecclesiastes 6 was taught as the dark twin of chapter five's gift: a man given everything yet not the power to enjoy it (Poole), the stillborn comparison as extreme rhetoric about length without satisfaction, appetite that never fills, and wandering desire against the sight of the eyes (Gill); the question was whether we can receive what we have. John 3:1-15 was the heart: Nicodemus by night (Augustine), anothen as again and from above, the renovation of the whole nature (Calvin), water and Spirit against Ezekiel 36, pneuma as wind and Spirit (Spurgeon 1877, a Ligonier devotional), and the bronze serpent (Augustine); application: you cannot lift yourself, you must be born and look. James 4:1-10 covered wars from desires, adulterous friendship with the world (Henry, Gill), God opposing the proud and giving more grace (Bengel), and the drumbeat of commands from submit to humble yourselves.
threads: John 3:16-21 tomorrow: Jesus keeps speaking after Nicodemus goes quiet; light and darkness, recall that Nicodemus came by night.
James 4:11-17 tomorrow: speaking against one another and the vapor of life; recall the tongue and humility.
Ecclesiastes 7:1-14 tomorrow: the house of mourning; recall the unenjoyed wealth of chapter six.
Running theme: receiving what is given versus reaching. Avoid repeating Augustine's night and Light line, Calvin's renovation of the whole nature, Spurgeon's free agent, Bengel's resists the proud.
